entries.title: Ukraine: Russian strikes injure several in Kyiv, Odesa
entries.summary: Russian airstrikes hit apartment buildings and warehouses in Ukraine, injuring several people, including a child.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Russian strikes injure several in Kyiv, Odesa

September 17, 2026

Russian airstrikes hit apartment buildings and warehouses in Ukraine, injuring several people, including a child.

Russian airstrikes on Ukrainian cities of Kyiv and Odesa injured at least 13 people early on Thursday, Ukrainian officials said, as the war heads toward its fifth winter.

"An air raid alert has been declared in Kyiv due to the threat of missile strikes. We urge residents to proceed to the nearest shelters," the Kyiv City Military Administration wrote on Telegram.

At least 10 people were wounded in the Ukrainian capital, officials said on the messaging app. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said apartment buildings and warehouses had been damaged in the latest strikes, and that debris also fell near a petrol station.

News agencies such as Reuters and AFP cited witnesses hearing "strong" explosions in Kyiv.

In the Black Sea port City of Odesa, at least three people were injured when a Russian strike hit a 19-story apartment building, authorities said. A child was among those injured.

Both Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent months, along with the continued use of drones, to strike inside each other's territories.

Mediated talks ahead?

The strikes continue even as Russia and Ukraine recently signalled their readiness to resume talks under US mediation. Earlier this week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office said officials were preparing for talks in October. Similar signals came from Moscow, which said it did not rule out such a possibility.

The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.

entries.title: Trump threatens EU with further sanctions over Canada
entries.summary: The EU had signaled that Canada is poised to become the bloc's first associate member. Trump called the idea both "laughable" and a "hostile act."
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump threatens EU with further sanctions over Canada

September 17, 2026

The EU had signaled that Canada is poised to become the bloc's first associate member. Trump called the idea both "laughable" and a "hostile act."

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday responded to the European Union's plans to add Canada as an associate member with threats and ridicule.

During her annual speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was opening the door for ‌Canada ⁠to ⁠become its first associate member.

Such a relationship to the bloc does not currently exist and would have to be created from scratch.

How did Trump respond to Canada's EU associate membership idea?

In comments to reporters on Wednesday, Trump said the idea could become a "hostile act." He threatened to impose sanctions on the EU in response.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina.

The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."

Why is Canada turning to the EU?

The potential Canadian EU associate membership comes as Trump, during his second term in office, has shaken Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor to the core.

Canada was among the first victims of Trump's tariff policy.

Tensions escalated between Ottawa and Washington after trade talks broke down last month, with Trump imposing further sanctions on Canada and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowing to respond in kind.

Washington's transatlantic ties have also suffered under Trump, most notably after the US president's push to take control of the Arctic island of Greenland, which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

The EU was also hit by Trump's wide tariffs, as were most countries worldwide, but the two sides reached a trade agreement to bring them down.

entries.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
entries.summary: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.
entries.content:
September 17, 2026

A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.

"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."

How the disaster unfolded

The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.

The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.

Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.

How did this happen?

It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.

Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.

Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.

Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.

In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.

An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.

Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.

A disaster beyond adaptation

Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.

Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.

The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.

"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.

"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

entries.title: US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
entries.summary: The sanctions package is considered the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to the White House. Measures in the bill could lead to secondary sanctions on India, China and Iran.
entries.content:
United States of America

US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill

September 17, 2026

The sanctions package is considered the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to the White House. Measures in the bill could lead to secondary sanctions on India, China and Iran.

The US Republican-led US House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine.

The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.

The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it.

What does the sanctions package against Russia entail?

The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.

More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures.

The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.

It was drafted in April 2025 by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July.

But Trump had delayed the bill's passage, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress.

Who opposed the bill and why?

Democrats who voted for the bill broke ranks with the party leadership, which argues the legislation expands Trump's tariff powers and that the president already has the power to sanction Russia should he choose to.

"What this legislation will do ​is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash ⁠tariffs on the American people," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a speech on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, some Republicans opposed to the bill were wary of compounded tariffs further increasing consumer prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.

The bill's supporters say it is integral to keeping up the pressure on Russia.

It has been celebrated by Ukrainian activists. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and even watched an early procedural vote from the chamber.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports
entries.summary: The center-left opposition won the Swedish elections by a very slim margin, the public broadcaster reported after 99% of the votes were counted. Thorny negotiations await the bloc even if the result is confirmed.
entries.content:
Sweden

Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports

September 17, 2026

The center-left opposition won the Swedish elections by a very slim margin, the public broadcaster reported after 99% of the votes were counted. Thorny negotiations await the bloc even if the result is confirmed.

Sweden's center-left opposition bloc looks set to win the most votes in the country's parliamentary election, albeit by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday with 99% of the votes counted.

As of 1647 GMT, with fewer than 1% of votes left to count, the center-left bloc was ahead by just 26,169 votes.

The bloc is led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, the party that ruled Sweden for most of the 20th century.

If the results are confirmed, it would usher in a change in government from the right-wing bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.

What do we know about the Swedish election results so far?

Data from Sweden's election authority shows Kristersson's bloc was on track to win 174 seats, against 175 seats for the center-left. Both Kristersson and Andersson have said they would be open to exploring coalition options.

"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we ​can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," ⁠SVT ​said.

The election authority was counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, a process expected to continue until Thursday.

Even with Andersson's slim lead, her bloc is bracing for tough negotiations before forming any government, especially amid deep divisions between the liberal Center Party and the socialist Left Party.

After the 2022 elections, it took 37 days to form a government, which was considerably shorter than in 2018, when the process took 134 days.

Parliament cannot vote in a new prime minister before September 29.

entries.title: US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
entries.summary: In an attempt to address the persistently high inflation in the world's largest economy, the US Federal Reserve increased interest rates by 25 basis points. The president, on the other hand, said they should be cut.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

In an attempt to address the persistently high inflation in the world's largest economy, the US Federal Reserve increased interest rates by 25 basis points. The president, on the other hand, said they should be cut.

The US Federal Reserve (Fed) on Wednesday raised interest rates by 25 basis points in an attempt to tackle stubbornly high inflation in the world's largest economy.

This move is sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has called for lower rates and who recently nominated Kevin Warsh to the post of Federal Reserve Chair.

"Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," Warsh told a press conference.

Warsh has served as Fed Chair since May and during his confirmation process, he had assured Congress that central bank policymakers would "have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation." 

"Today's policy action will support a ​timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," Warsh added.

The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.

Trump had promised to lower prices in his 2024 election campaign, but things turned out differently after his inauguration. The US now faces the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom.

After the announcement of the rate increase, Trump said US interest rates should ‌be 1% or lower and that the rates ⁠should be cut fast.

"I ... talked to Kevin," Trump said. "And I said you might as well vote with the board because ​it's not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing."

Fed plans to 'stay in our lane'

Since his appointment to the job, speculation circulated around which direction Warsh would take the Fed, as Trump has pressured the institution to follow his lead.

But on Wednesday, Warsh joined the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, saying it had been made independent of what the market may be doing.

"We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation," he said. "I'll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision."

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane," Warsh said. "We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That's how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them."

Borrowers will feel some impact

The raise in interest rates will affect those who borrow money to make large purchases, such as a home, car or large appliance.

The new rate will also raise monthly payments and costs for those who are already paying interest on credit card debt.

Currently, household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So many households will not feel the burden on borrowing in the short term.

But the move could be good for those who are saving, as interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit will rise.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation
entries.summary: Oktoberfest's traditional beer mug, the Mass, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) at this year's festival in Munich.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

Oktoberfest's traditional beer mug, the Mass, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) at this year's festival in Munich.

The price of a liter of beer at Munich's Oktoberfest has risen fivefold since 1985, far outpacing overall inflation in Germany, according to an analysis by UniCredit's chief economist in Germany.

A Mass, the traditional 1-liter (2.1-pint) serving at Oktoberfest, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) this year. In 1985, it cost about 6.25 Deutschmarks, equivalent to €3.20 after conversion at the fixed euro exchange rate.

The figures were analyzed by UniCredit economist Andreas Rees ahead of the opening of the world's largest beer festival on Saturday.

Beer prices at Oktoberfest have increased by around 400% since 1985, according to Rees, using data from Munich's statistical office.

Consumer prices across Germany, by comparison, have risen by around 120% over the same period.

What determines the Mass' price?

This year's increase is considerably more modest. The average price of a Mass is up 2.4% from last year, below Germany's expected overall inflation rate of close to 3%.

"Beer prices at the Oktoberfest depend on a peculiar cocktail of harvests, energy prices, wages, tent costs, security and the willingness of millions of visitors to spend generously," Rees said.

Although the trend has been one of sharply rising prices, this year's Mass saw a price of 2.4% compared to 2025, the smallest increase in two decades.

Rees explained that ingredient prices could be playing a role, as hops have become cheaper while malting-barley prices have stabilized.

Festival draws millions

Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world. Locals and tourists alike wear the traditional Bavarian lederhosen and dirndl dresses on the festival grounds.

The festival dates back to 1810, and it takes place at the Wiesn, a the local dialect abbreviation for Theresienwiese, the fairgrounds in Munich named in honor of Crown Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen.

This Saturday, Munich will celebrate the 191st Oktoberfest, expecting somewhere between 6 and 7 million visitors.

The party begins when the city's mayor opens the first barrel in a ceremony officially marking the opening of the festival.

entries.title: UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
entries.summary: Residents of Piddington, a tiny, remote village in Oxfordshire in England, have staged a "referendum" on leaving the UK. They are objecting to plans to open an asylum reception center at a disused military base nearby.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest

September 16, 2026

Residents of Piddington, a tiny, remote village in Oxfordshire in England, have staged a "referendum" on leaving the UK. They are objecting to plans to open an asylum reception center at a disused military base nearby.

An English village of about 350 people has voted to "secede" from the United Kingdom, in a symbolic protest against government plans to set up an asylum reception center nearby. 

Residents of Piddington, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Oxford, celebrated with a placard reading "Principality of Piddington" near the village road sign on Wednesday.

They oppose plans, still under review, to house asylum seekers in a disused military base, MoD Bicester (Site A).

What happened in the tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote?

The village's parish council said that 312 people cast ballots in the vote, a turnout of almost 92%.

Participants in the vote, which had no legal basis, were asked to agree or disagree with the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination."

Of them, 285 voted to secede, 26 voted against, and one spoiled their ballot.

Parish council chair Tim McNally said that, going forward, the village would identify as the "Principality of Piddington."

"For us, it's about proportiality," McNally told Sky News. "How does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?"

He accused the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through."

An Oxfordshire County Council official told the BBC the plan risked making the village and the facility a "lightning rod" for potentially violent far-right protests.

The vote attracted the attention of self-styled anti-migration "influencers" online.

How did the government react?

The Labour government has been trying to move asylum seekers housed in hotels, an unpopular legacy they inherited from previous British governments, into disused military facilities by 2029.

This follows repeated protests at or near hotels and rented accommodation used for the purpose.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who only recently took over the rapidly rotating top job in British politics, promised to "look at the issues raised by the community and in the referendum."

But he also said that the "vast majority" of British people backed a government plan to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels and argued that it was "fair" to locate holding centers around the country.

Speaking to the BBC, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said a former military base was "a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels or rented accommodation.

One drawback with disused military bases, however, is that they are often intentionally placed in remote and rural areas. This can be ideal for military training and activity, but is less obviously suited to housing migrants with limited mobility and resources.

Migration and asylum have been contentious political issues in the UK for decades. But successive governments have faced particular pressure in recent years, with the populist right-wing Reform UK and Restore Britain parties gaining ground against the established political giants the Conservatives and Labour.

The most recent manifestation of this was anti-migrant protests in the coastal city of Portsmouth earlier this month. 

What does the government say about its plans for MoD Bicester?

In a Q+A published in July about its plans for Ministry of Defense (MoD) Bicester (Site A), the British government said the site "would provide basic, safe accommodation and would be designed to be largely self‑sufficient to minimize any impact on the local community."

It stressed the plan was still subject to feasibility studies, planning permission requirements and other red tape.

It didn't state how many people would be housed there, except to say: "The Home Office would take a phased approach to full occupancy, starting with smaller numbers at first."

It did specify that the facility would hold males aged 18-65.

The government said that if used, the site would be in operation for a minimum of 10 years. Relocating to military bases was "just the first step in the government’s work to exit hotels and source more appropriate accommodation to meet our statutory obligations," it said.

Safety for the local community, staff, and those accommodated on site would be "of the utmost importance," it said. The facility would be monitored round the clock by a security provider and via surveillance footage.

It would also be "designed to be as self-sufficient as possible including laundry facilities and communal spaces," the British government said.

entries.title: Chancellor Merz seeks CDU support as AfD encroaches
entries.summary: Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, many are expressing doubts about the party's leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. But the CDU doesn't appear to have a viable alternative.
entries.content:
Germany

Chancellor Merz seeks CDU support as AfD encroaches

September 16, 2026

Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, many are expressing doubts about the party's leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. But the CDU doesn't appear to have a viable alternative.

Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers (about 1,100 miles) north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various countries had gathered there for the European Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.

When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent.

"That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.

Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

Why is Merz so unpopular?

Another heavy defeat looks likely in the state election coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low 7%. Failure to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.

The election earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt was won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, in this central German state.

Before taking office, Merz promised he would cut support for the AfD "in half." Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?

Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."

One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."

When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.

"You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now," said SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese on the Welt TV channel. "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."

Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst

But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.

SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.

Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag.

However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.

Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the chancellor."

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

The statement was signed by all eight premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Pivotal state elections coming up

So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down.

If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.

Merz's schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources have confirmed.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?
entries.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Carney is known for standing up to US President Donald Trump. Now he wants to forge a "unique alliance" with Europe. But what could such a partnership look like?
entries.content:
Europe

Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?

September 16, 2026

Canadian Prime Minister Carney is known for standing up to US President Donald Trump. Now he wants to forge a "unique alliance" with Europe. But what could such a partnership look like?

Before taking off for Europe, CanadianPrime Minister Mark Carney had set the tone for his visit, saying he was seeking to build a "unique alliance" with the EU. The Wall Street Journal similarly reported that Canada was considering becoming an "associate member" of the EU, while not aiming for full membership.

In her State of the European Union address on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen indicated that she was indeed open to such an expanded partnership.

"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," she said, addressing European lawmakers and Carney in Strasbourg, France. "That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work."

Von der Leyen said a EU-Canada partnership would cover a broad range of areas including advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.

Carney is expected to outline his vision for future relations between the EU and Canada during a speech at the European Parliament on Thursday.

What degree of collaboration could be possible between the EU and Canada?

EU member states are closely integrated economically, sharing a common market, trade and customs policy. When it comes to establishing ties with non-EU countries, a list of different options present themselves. They range from free trade agreements that scrap tariffs and trade barriers, to association agreements which may include political elements, to far-reaching economic arrangements such as participation in the common European market, as is the case for Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.

The EU has already negotiated association agreements with Turkey, Israel and Ukraine. These have different objectives and may or may not mark a preliminary step toward full membership.

Patrick Leblond, an expert on international economic relations at the University of Ottawa, urges a little more caution around the term "association agreement." He considers it unlikely that Canada would adopt European laws or join the EU single market or customs union, which would mean imposing common external tariffs.

Leblond says Carney is likely more interested in forming a kind of alliance that deepens cooperation on issues of economic security and defense.

Closer defense cooperation?

"We have, in a way, taken the US [security] umbrella for granted on both sides. We have underinvested in our militaries," Leblond told DW.

He added that the focus was now on joining forces, for example in the production of military equipment and the development of new technologies.

Security analyst Anand Sundar of the European Council on Foreign Relations also sees great potential for European-Canadian cooperation when it comes to defense. Canada spends about 70% of its defense budget on US-made equipment, according to Sundar. Carney wants to change that, the analyst said, as it would pay off for Canadians to be part of European defense projects to get "more bang for their buck."

Canada has joined the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program. It provides EU member states with up to €150 billion ($173 billion, CA$ 241 billion) in loans for the joint procurement of military equipment. To qualify for funding, no more than 35% of the cost of the components can come from countries outside the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) or Ukraine. Yet because Canada joined the SAFE program by paying a fee, more lenient procurement rules apply to its companies.

Nevertheless, Canadian companies still face significant hurdles for producing and purchasing weapons in partnership with European firms, Sundar told DW. The big question is how far the EU is willing to relax its own rules, the expert says, which could also have implications for non-EU countries, such as the United Kingdom or Norway.

'Underrated defense power'

"But the biggest draw for the European Union is really the fact that that Canada is an underrated defense power," Sundar told DW.

Canada, the expert added, spends more on defense than the 14 smallest EU member states combined.

The North American country invests 2% of its gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, Sundar said, with an increase expected in the coming years. Canada, like other NATO countries, has committed to spending a total of 5% of its GDP on defense by 2035, of which 3.5% will go towards military equipment and the remaining 1.5% towards other defense-related areas.

Protecting critical infrastructure

The EU and Canada also intend to discuss potential cooperation in the field of critical infrastructure expansion, such as the joint operation of space satellites or maintenance of fiber-optic cables in the North Atlantic, Leblond told DW. The goal here, too, is to become less dependent on the US and its companies. Moreover, Canada has oil and gas reserves that could meet some of the bloc's energy demands.

Trade relations between both have already been codified through the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force on a provisional basis in September 2017. The agreement eliminates nearly all tariffs between the EU and Canada, while also ensuring mutual market access for industrial goods, agricultural products and services. It even enables European companies to participate in public tenders in Canada.

Economic analyst Leblond, however, believes that CETA's potential has not yet been fully realized. He says many Canadian companies still tend to focus on the US and less on Europe. He believes it is the government's responsibility to provide more information about CETA and the opportunities it offers, saying the level of exchange envisaged in this format could also be intensified.

Why is Carney seeking closer ties with Europe?

In January, Carney delivered a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in which he warned of a "rupture in the world order," calling on the middle powers to act together.

"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he said.

Indeed, in recent weeks, the US-Canda trade war has continued escalating.

Even though it is clear that Canada cannot sever ties with the US, there is a growing belief inside Canada that the country needs additional allies, Leblond told DW. And the Europeans are considered trustworthy, he added.

Ultimately, the Canadians would want to see such an alliance, whatever form it may take, translate into concrete initiatives and projects through which Europeans and Canadians can help one another.
